survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses three waves of OECD PISA administered to 15-year-olds in Italy (2012, 2015, 2018) and relies on PISA’s two-stage sampling design (random selection of students from non-randomly selected schools). The manuscript states that national sampling weights are post-processed and added to the dataset by OECD to increase representativeness, and the analysis further applies inverse probability weighting (IPW) based on propensity scores for track selection (Liberal Arts vs STEM). In the matching step, inverse probability weights are derived from a logistic regression of track membership on pre-high-school student and parental characteristics, and then used to compute weighted differences in means. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not specify a single named PISA weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), so the weighting strategy is described at the methodological level rather than by an explicit weight field name.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe a missing-data strategy for the analytic variables (e.g., whether cases with missing covariates were excluded or whether any imputation was used for missing questionnaire/background items). While the study does impute TIMSS/PIRLS-based “implied” achievement for robustness checks, this is not a documented general missing-data procedure for the full set of PISA covariates and outcomes. This omission limits reproducibility because missingness handling can affect propensity-score estimation and the stability of decomposition results.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses three public-use PISA datasets (2012, 2015, 2018) for Italy obtained from INVALSI. The analytic sample is restricted to students whose national “pathway”/track can be identified and who are in either the Liberal Arts track or the technical track (STEM), yielding 841 Liberal Arts and 1968 technical students. Prior PISA waves are excluded because cohorts were schooled under a different regime (law 1/2009) making track identification impossible. The study further constructs propensity scores using pre-high-school characteristics (female, grade repeater, immigration status, books at home, region, and location) and then applies inverse probability weighting for the matching step; robustness checks re-estimate models using imputed TIMSS/PIRLS scores linked via exact covariate matching on the same variables.

main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement gap (STEM vs Liberal Arts)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Inverse probability matching: Unmatched difference = -8.4 PISA points (t = -2.8, p < 0.001); Matched difference = -22.0 PISA points (t = -7.4, p < 0.001). Achievement decomposition: endowments effect = -11.7; coefficients effect = 14.4.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012-2018 (Italy) the study leveraged gender, books at home, region, location, and immigration status to estimate the STEM–Liberal Arts reading achievement gap via inverse probability matching, finding that Liberal Arts students have lower reading achievement than STEM students after adjustment (matched difference: -22.0 PISA points). This indicates that increasing technical coursework does not produce a verbal-reasoning trade-off and may instead generate positive spillovers into reading, though the study’s causal interpretation is limited by the lack of a fully documented missing-data strategy and by reliance on observational matching.

main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement gap (STEM vs Liberal Arts)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Inverse probability matching: Unmatched difference = -44.2 PISA points (t = -14.4, p < 0.001); Matched difference = -50.1 PISA points (t = -16.2, p < 0.001). Achievement decomposition: coefficients effect = 41.9; endowments effect = 4.0.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012-2018 (Italy) the study leveraged gender, books at home, region, location, and grade repeater to estimate the STEM–Liberal Arts math achievement gap via inverse probability matching, finding that STEM students outperform Liberal Arts students and the gap remains large after adjustment (matched difference: -50.1 PISA points). This indicates that STEM-track instructional requirements are associated with higher numerical achievement without evidence of a compensating verbal loss, though the study’s decomposition-based attribution depends on the observational track-selection model and the paper does not report a missing-data handling procedure.

main_findings.target_variable: Science achievement gap (STEM vs Liberal Arts)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Inverse probability matching: Unmatched difference = -24.8 PISA points (t = -8.0, p < 0.001); Matched difference = -32.9 PISA points (t = -10.6, p < 0.001). Achievement decomposition: coefficients effect = 25.5; endowments effect = -5.7.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012-2018 (Italy) the study leveraged gender, books at home, region, location, and immigration status to estimate the STEM–Liberal Arts science achievement gap via inverse probability matching, finding that STEM students have substantially higher science achievement after adjustment (matched difference: -32.9 PISA points). This indicates that STEM-track curricular emphasis is linked to stronger science outcomes, and that the STEM advantage is driven primarily by differences in returns to educational inputs rather than by differences in observable student and family endowments, though causal claims remain constrained by the absence of a documented missing-data strategy.

data.outcome_summary: The paper analyzes Italy’s secondary academic tracking by comparing students in the Liberal Arts versus technical (STEM) track using OECD PISA test scores from 2012, 2015, and 2018 (15-year-olds; Italy only). The analytic sample contains 841 Liberal Arts and 1968 STEM students, and the study applies inverse probability weighting to adjust for observable track-selection differences using propensity scores based on student and parental characteristics (e.g., gender, grade repetition, immigration status, books at home, region, and location). After matching, STEM students score higher in math (−50.1 PISA points difference) and science (−32.9), while reading shows no trade-off and instead a larger negative gap for Liberal Arts (−22.0). Decomposition results indicate that math and science gaps are mainly explained by coefficients/returns effects, while reading’s endowments and coefficients components move in opposite directions. Limitations include the lack of a reported general missing-data handling strategy and the fact that the study’s causal interpretation relies on observational matching rather than randomized track assignment.
